description: Straight from Cuiabá, MT (the center of South America), the Capivaláxias crew has landed! We blend the chill, resilient nature of the capybara with a passion for tech and out-of-the-box problem-solving. We believe the best solutions are built in a relaxed environment fueled by high-energy collaboration.
summary:
SkyBlink is a public web tool that turns SPHEREx observations of any patch of sky into a short movie, one frame per observing season, so anyone can see what moves. Type a position (or open a shared link), and SkyBlink finds every SPHEREx exposure of that region in the NASA/IPAC archive, stacks each season into one clean frame, and plays them in order with the same brightness scale.

In 1930, Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto during the search for "Planet X" by blinking two photographic plates back and forth. SkyBlink does the same with infrared images from SPHEREx, in a browser.

What makes it trustworthy is that it also says when not to believe your eyes. Every frame carries quality checks: saturated stars, frames built from too few exposures, and background stars that shift between seasons (an alignment problem, not real motion). For the object at the center, SkyBlink measures its motion with an error bar and, when the target is named, compares it with the Gaia catalog prediction for the same dates, parallax included. On Barnard's Star, the measured motion is 10.47 ± 0.34 arcsec/yr against a predicted 10.65 arcsec/yr.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

You give SkyBlink a sky position (RA/Dec in degrees, or in hours, minutes and seconds) and a field of view. It returns a looping movie of that region: one frame per SPHEREx observing season, all on the same pixel grid and brightness scale, with a fixed crosshair at the center. Every position is a shareable link (?ra=&dec=&fov=). Next to the movie, SkyBlink reports what the data can and cannot support: quality alerts per frame, and the measured motion of the central object with its uncertainty and, for named targets, the catalog prediction.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Find the data: query the IRSA SIA2 service for every SPHEREx exposure covering the position (DR1 and QR3 collections, all six detectors).

2. Group into seasons: SPHEREx maps the whole sky about every six months; exposures more than 30 days apart start a new season.

3. Download small cutouts through the IRSA cutout service, cached on disk.

4. Clean each exposure: subtract the zodiacal-light model and the residual background; mask bad pixels using the SPHEREx FLAGS bitmask read from each file's header.

5. Stack each season on a common grid at the native 6.15 arcsec pixel with an inverse-variance weighted mean.

6. Render with one brightness scale per detector, so changes between frames are changes in the data, not in contrast.

7. Check before you believe: alerts for no coverage, a single season, few exposures, saturated targets and alignment drift.

8. Measure the motion of the central source on each stacked frame, corrected by reference stars, and compare it with the catalog prediction at the same mean exposure epochs, including annual parallax.

VALIDATION (SPHEREx D6, 4.4-5.0 micrometers)

- Barnard's Star: measured 10.47 +/- 0.34 arcsec/yr vs predicted 10.65 arcsec/yr (-0.5 sigma). The result does not depend on the field of view: 10.47 (6 arcmin), 10.53 (15 arcmin), 10.45 (30 arcmin).

- Epsilon Indi B: 4.67 +/- 0.38 vs 4.10 arcsec/yr (+1.5 sigma), with an alignment warning in one season.

- RW Aurigae: 0.49 +/- 0.62 arcsec/yr, consistent with no motion, as expected.

- WISE 0855-0714 and R Draconis: no motion reported, because the signal is too weak or the core has no usable centroid. SkyBlink refuses to report numbers it cannot defend.

- Saturation alerts: a naive rule had an 8.5% false-alarm chance per frame; our rule (at least 25% and at least 2 exposures saturated at the target) brings it to about 3 x 10^-8.

- A finding: stars move so much that catalog positions go out of date. The challenge's position for WISE 0855 is about 2 arcmin from where the brown dwarf is now, and Wikipedia's J2000 position for Barnard's Star is about 4.5 arcmin off. SkyBlink shows where they really are.

KNOWN LIMITS

Each season mixes wavelengths within a detector band, so brightness changes between frames are not a variability measurement. Season stacks erase fast solar-system movers: a distant planet would smear within a season and jump out of the field between seasons, so hunting Planet X needs single exposures followed along predicted paths, our next step.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Anyone can watch the infrared sky change without downloading or processing FITS files, in English or Portuguese, on a phone or a laptop. It teaches the right habit: a difference you see is a question, and the tool shows the evidence for and against it. It keeps working when the archive is slow or down: discovery results, cutouts and finished movies are cached on disk. It could feed citizen science projects like Backyard Worlds. And it works for any point in the sky, for anyone in the world: it runs in a browser, in English and Portuguese, with open-source code and a public API that other tools, classrooms and citizen-science projects can reuse.

NEXT STEPS

Spectra of the central source across the 102 SPHEREx bands, a single-exposure mode for solar-system objects, difference images, Gaia overlays and a name search that places moving objects at their current position.

TOOLS

Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Astropy, Astroquery, PyVO, reproject, NumPy, Pillow, HTTPX, pytest (140 tests), Docker, Fly.io. Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Motion, three.js, Vercel.

Source code: https://github.com/carvalhocaio/skyblink

Public API: https://skyblink-api.fly.dev

Try Barnard's Star directly: https://skyblink-swart.vercel.app/?ra=269.4462&dec=4.7682&fov=6
